goal_text: Write a PRD for my side project

nodes.title: Nail the problem statement
nodes.one_liner: What problem, for whom, why it matters now

nodes.title: Who's the user, really?
nodes.one_liner: Defining users and their concrete jobs-to-be-done

nodes.title: What are you actually betting on?
nodes.one_liner: Surfacing your core assumptions and hypotheses

nodes.title: Draw the scope line
nodes.one_liner: What's in v1, what's explicitly out and why

nodes.title: How will you know it worked?
nodes.one_liner: Defining success criteria and signals to watch

nodes.title: Name the risks and unknowns
nodes.one_liner: Open questions that could break the plan

nodes.title: A lean PRD structure to reuse
nodes.one_liner: Section skeleton fitting a solo thinking doc

outline.rationale: The user already knows what a PRD is and wants a structural thinking scaffold for a solo side project, so I skipped basics and all team-alignment sections (sign-off, handoffs, approvals). The outline front-loads the clarifying-thinking sections the understanding flagged as most valuable: problem, users, scope, and success criteria. I added an "assumptions/bets" node and a "risks/unknowns" node because for a solo founder these force honesty better than stakeholder-oriented sections would. The "solution shape" node is framed to avoid over-speccing, matching the scaffold-not-spec intent. The final node gives a reusable lean structure so the framework generalizes across product types, honoring the "general-purpose, unnamed project" signal. Nodes are ordered by dependency (problem → users → bets → scope → solution → success → risks → structure) and are largely non-overlapping.
